title: Giant branch sculptures hold through entanglement physics, not weaving skill
dek: An 81-year-old sculptor builds installations dozens of feet tall from tons of branches without a single nail or rope, using the same entanglement mechanics as bird nests—thin, long branches lock tighter when tangled, while short thick ones stay loose.
why: For anyone interested in craftsmanship, structural physics, and interdisciplinary science—the interview is detail-rich and dense with substance, with almost no filler.
who: Anyone who loves craftsmanship, installation art, structural mechanics, or wants to know why willows are the traditional ninth-anniversary gift.
skip: Around 56:36, a long section of listener questions and thank-yous can be skipped without losing the main narrative.

points.h: Tapered branches create the illusion of motion
points.body: Patrick builds sculptures in stages: first the structure—dig holes, bury thick posts, build scaffolding, bend them to shape, always step one. Then comes aesthetics, finally "makeup"—like removing stray lines from a drawing, inserting small branches to hide flaws and make surfaces look natural. The motion illusion technique uses the natural taper of branches: arranged in one direction like a pencil line thickening and thinning, they create a wind-blown effect without precise preliminary sketches.

points.h: Willow branches must be harvested before bulldozers arrive
points.body: Patrick doesn't simply buy materials. It's a race against time: on the ‘belt lines’ where urban expansion clears new ground, saplings are ‘brides waiting to be wed’, vanishing once bulldozers arrive. His team stops on highway shoulders for promising saplings, sometimes driving a hundred miles to negotiate with landowners. Permissions are their own challenge—the daughter says yes but the father refuses, and suddenly it's a family war. Steady sources include wastewater treatment plants, forestry clearance sites, and Duke Forest.

points.h: Nail-free sculptures hold through entanglement physics alone
points.body: The structures hold for decades without a single nail or rope, pure entanglement physics. Two research papers explain the mechanism: one studies California black soldier flies that use spiral waves to knot and instantly unknot themselves; another CT-scanned a bird nest and found that rod-shaped objects with high aspect ratios form strong entanglement zones—exactly the physics Patrick relies on when selecting branches.

points.h: Forty years away from home produced 335 major sculptures
points.body: Patrick works ten months a year, three weeks per sculpture, moving continuously for forty years with barely any time at home. At 78 he decided to slow down. Now 81, he's completed approximately 335 major works, each consuming 3-4 tons of branches—equivalent to a full railcar of material.

points.h: The most useful branches are the ones that hook others
points.body: When asked about willow's flexibility, Patrick says the secret isn't just flexibility but side branches: his team hunts for branches that ‘hook onto everything’ when dragged through brush—that annoying entanglement quality is exactly what locks branches together and holds the structure. Some willows shed side branches immediately and are unusable; they need branches with abundant, persistent, elastic side branches—the more elastic, the better.

points.h: Plant willows too close and roots will rupture your pipes
points.body: Listeners ask about planting willows in their yards. Patrick cautions that willows have vigorous, water-seeking roots; experts recommend at least 20 meters (60 feet) from foundations or pipes. One listener shares a hard lesson: their downspout was blocked by willow roots, requiring thousands of dollars to replace the pipe—so before settling into meditation under a weeping willow, measure your distance carefully.

points.h: Artwork names require Indigenous elders' approval and participation
points.body: For a project at Northern Illinois University, the team had to seek approval from local Lakota elders before using willows. The condition: the elders would name the work. The naming process became a deep conversation: was ‘dancing willow’ about branches moved by wind or the willow's own will to participate? The final name—chan shasha wachipi (dancing willow)—reflects this shared meaning-making.

points.h: Completion is determined by intuition, not by schedule
points.body: Completion is by intuition, not by schedule. Like polishers gradually making scratches finer, he smooths branch surfaces incrementally. As finish approaches, Patrick tells volunteers an hour or two before completion, but nobody wants to stop—the work is too satisfying. At the end, everyone walks around the finished sculpture in circumambulation. In New Harmony, Indiana, the whole town spontaneously turned out to witness the moment it was done.
